note.note:
Consult Summary:
- 25–? year-old female (Tim/Kim) presents with 2 days of gradually worsening lower abdominal (suprapubic) burning pain, associated with nausea, feeling hot/sweaty, and possible pink urine.
- Clinician suspects urinary tract infection among other causes (gut-related or pregnancy-related); Trimethoprim prescribed empirically; pregnancy test and clinical follow-up recommended.

Problem List:

Issue 1:
- Lower abdominal (just below the belly button) burning pain for ~2 days, gradual onset, constant and worsening; sore to palpation.
- Associated symptoms: mild nausea, feeling hot and sweaty.
- Bowel history: recent constipation last week that has resolved; current bowel movements reported as normal; no diarrhea or vomiting.
- Systems review pertinent negatives: no cough, no shortness of breath, no palpitations, no headache, no visual changes.
- Examination findings: none documented in transcript.

Issue 2:
- Possible urinary involvement: patient noted pink-colored urine and increased urinary frequency; unclear if frank hematuria — patient states “maybe” blood.
- No dysuria or burning on urination reported.
- Clinician impression: urinary tract infection considered as a possible cause and discussed as part of differential (also gut-related causes and pregnancy-related causes).
- No urine testing results documented; clinician offered to organize tests but patient preferred to start antibiotics.

Issue 3:
- Pregnancy consideration: patient has Implanon inserted ~1 year ago; sexually active with same partner, last sexual activity 4 days ago; last period ~2 weeks ago; last STI screen normal ~6 months ago.
- Clinician advised pregnancy test to exclude pregnancy-related causes.
- No pregnancy test result documented.

Medications:
- Implanon (contraceptive implant) — dose/route/frequency not applicable.
- Trimethoprim — prescribed; dose/route/frequency not clearly documented in transcript.
  - Transcript contains conflicting clinician statements: “you can take two tablets” AND “one tablet twice a day for three days” (conflict noted).
- Paracetamol recommended for pain (dose/route/frequency not documented).
- Cranberry juice recommended as supportive measure (non-pharmacologic).

Allergies:
- None mentioned.

Past Medical History:
- No prior surgeries.
- No other chronic medical conditions documented.
- Not on other regular medications aside from Implanon.

Social History:
- Lives in a share house with two roommates.
- Employed as an accountant.
- Sexually active with a single partner.
- Smoking: denies.
- Alcohol: social use, not excessive per patient.

Preventative History:
- STI screen normal approximately 6 months ago.
- No other preventative care (cervical screening, mammogram, PSA, FOBT, BMD, vaccinations, optometry, skin check) documented.

Physical Examination:
- No vital signs documented.
- No formal abdominal or other examination findings recorded in the transcript.
- Patient reports subjective feeling of being hot and sweaty; no measured fever recorded.

Plan:
- Start empiric antibiotic therapy with Trimethoprim as prescribed; prescription to be sent to pharmacy for patient to collect.
  - Note: dosing instruction in transcript is conflicting; clarify dosing if required before administration.
- Advise pregnancy test to be performed to exclude pregnancy-related causes.
- Supportive measures: paracetamol for analgesia, maintain adequate oral fluids, consider cranberry juice for urinary symptoms.
- Safety-netting and follow-up: patient to return or contact clinician in a few days if symptoms do not improve or if they worsen (worsening abdominal pain, persistent fever/hot sweats, vomiting, or other concerning symptoms).
- Clinician had offered to organize initial tests (e.g., urine/pregnancy testing) today; patient elected to start antibiotics instead — arrange testing as feasible/encouraged.

document_quality:
- Missing but clinically expected elements: vital signs (temperature, heart rate, blood pressure), abdominal examination findings, urine dipstick/microscopy/culture results, pregnancy test result, explicit confirmed antibiotic dosing and route, complete medication reconciliation.
- Internal conflicts from transcript: inconsistent antibiotic instruction — clinician states both “take two tablets” and “one tablet twice a day for three days” regarding Trimethoprim (conflict noted).
- Transcript quality: generally clear and understandable with occasional stuttering and brief interruptions; key clinical information documented.
